lessons.title: The financial statements
lessons.why: Statement questions show up on every exam, and they're the base for most roleplay cases.

lessons.title: Financial institutions and markets
lessons.why: These three finance-cluster PIs appeared 14 times across the three practice exams.

lessons.title: The economy, globalization and reading stock data
lessons.why: These four PIs appeared 19 times combined. Stock-table questions are easy points once you know the columns.

lessons.title: Time value of money, credit and personal finance
lessons.why: Expect about 2 math questions from FI:238, and personal finance PIs fill several more.

lessons.title: Managerial accounting and costs
lessons.why: Six finance-cluster PIs with about 16 exam hits combined. Your daily practice roleplays lean on this too.

lessons.title: Financial-information management: scope, ethics, technology
lessons.why: Financial-Information Management is 9 questions at regionals, and most competitors never study it.

lessons.title: Financial analysis tools, budgeting apps, ratios
lessons.why: 18 exam hits. Ratio and analysis-technique questions are very predictable.

lessons.title: Risk management
lessons.why: Risk Management is 6 questions at regionals and 7 at states, and every PI here was tested 4 to 5 times.

lessons.title: Business law and compliance in finance
lessons.why: Business Law is 7 questions at regionals. The fraud-scheme terms are guaranteed points.

lessons.title: Corporate governance
lessons.why: Five governance PIs had 21 exam hits combined, the most of any topic.

lessons.title: Finance careers, networking, client service, CRM
lessons.why: 23 exam hits across these four PIs. Mostly common sense if you know the vocabulary.

lessons.title: Databases, data mining and information
lessons.why: NF:124 (advanced databases) was the single most tested PI: 7 hits in 3 exams.

lessons.title: Emotional intelligence and ethics at work
lessons.why: 9 questions at regionals. The answers are usually the most professional, mature choice.

lessons.title: Economics and operations
lessons.why: Together these are 12 questions at regionals.

lessons.title: Communication, customer relations and career skills
lessons.why: About 25 questions at regionals: Communications, Customer Relations and the general Professional Development PIs.

cards.d: Owners and managers use it to track performance, plan and budget, choose investments, meet legal requirements and earn the trust of lenders and investors.
cards.x: If a question describes comparing forecast (planned) results with actual results, the answer is "variance."

cards.d: Recording, classifying, summarizing and interpreting a business's financial transactions.
cards.x: Accounting keeps the records. Finance decides what to do with the money.

cards.d: Getting money (financing), putting it to work (investing in assets) and managing day-to-day money (working capital management).
cards.x: The finance function manages working capital and makes capital budgeting decisions.

cards.d: Shows revenue, expenses and net income (profit or loss) over a period of time. Also called the profit and loss statement (P&L).
cards.x: Lines in order: sales, cost of goods sold, gross profit, operating expenses, net profit.

cards.d: Revenue minus cost of goods sold.
cards.x: Gross profit comes before operating expenses. Net profit comes after them.

cards.d: A snapshot of what a business owns (assets), owes (liabilities) and is worth to its owners (equity) on one specific date.
cards.x: Prepared to show the business's current financial situation. Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity.

cards.d: Shows cash coming in and going out during a period, split into operating, investing and financing activities.
cards.x: Cash in: customer payments, loans received, owner investment, interest received, sale of assets. Cash out: supplier, wage and other expense payments, equipment purchases, loan repayments, dividends.

cards.d: Cash from the main business: customer payments in; supplier, wage and tax payments out.
cards.x: Healthy companies get most of their cash from operations, not from selling assets.

cards.d: Buying or selling long-term assets like equipment and buildings, and buying or selling investments.
cards.x: Buying a delivery truck = cash used in investing.

cards.d: Borrowing or repaying loans, owners putting money in or taking it out, issuing stock, paying dividends.
cards.x: Paying a dividend = financing outflow.

cards.d: Shows how owners' equity changed over a period: starting equity, plus net income and new investment, minus withdrawals or dividends, equals ending equity.
cards.x: Columns usually include contributed capital, retained earnings and dividends.

cards.d: Profits the company has earned and kept instead of paying out as dividends.
cards.x: Net income increases retained earnings. Dividends reduce them.

cards.d: Payments of profit to shareholders.
cards.x: On the equity statement they're recorded under Dividends and reduce retained earnings.

cards.d: Records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, whether or not cash has moved. Required by GAAP.
cards.x: Cash basis records only when cash changes hands.

cards.d: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles: the US accounting rules, set by the FASB.
cards.x: IFRS is the international version.

cards.d: Current assets turn into cash within a year (cash, receivables, inventory). Fixed assets are long-term (equipment, buildings) and are depreciated.
cards.x: Depreciation is a non-cash expense.

cards.d: How quickly assets can become cash to pay bills that are due soon.
cards.x: Profitable companies can still run out of cash. That's why the cash flow statement matters.

cards.d: Net income from the income statement flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet. Ending cash on the cash flow statement equals cash on the balance sheet.
cards.x: Explaining this link in a roleplay shows comprehensive understanding.

cards.d: An organization that handles financial transactions: banks, credit unions, insurance companies, investment firms.
cards.x: Their core job is moving money from savers to borrowers (financial intermediation).

cards.d: For-profit, shareholder-owned bank offering checking, savings and loans. The largest providers of banking services.
cards.x: Credit unions are not-for-profit and owned by their members.

cards.d: Not-for-profit, member-owned. Usually lower loan rates and fees than banks.
cards.x: Deposits insured by the NCUA, not the FDIC.

cards.d: Institution focused on savings accounts and home mortgages.
cards.x: Exam clue: an institution focused on home mortgages is a savings and loan.

cards.d: Helps companies and governments raise money by issuing stocks and bonds (underwriting), and advises on mergers.
cards.x: Investment banks find outside sources of money for firms.

cards.d: Sells policies that transfer risk: you pay a premium, they pay covered losses.
cards.x: Purpose: minimize financial risk.

cards.d: Buys and sells securities for clients.
cards.x: SIPC protects customers if the brokerage fails, not against market losses.

cards.d: International institution that provides loans, grants and advice to developing countries to reduce poverty.
cards.x: The IMF is different: it stabilizes the global monetary system and helps countries in currency crises.

cards.d: US central bank. Controls the money supply with open market operations, the discount rate and reserve requirements.
cards.x: Raising rates slows borrowing and inflation. Exams still list these three classic tools; in practice reserve requirements have been 0% since 2020, so the Fed works mainly through its federal funds rate target.

cards.d: Insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
Any organized system for buying and selling financial assets.
Market for short-term debt that matures within a year: Treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit.
cards.x: Treasury bills = money market.

cards.d: Market for long-term funds: stocks and bonds.
Primary: a company sells new securities directly to investors (an IPO). Secondary: investors trade those securities with each other afterward (NYSE, Nasdaq).
cards.x: Trading after the original sale = secondary market.

cards.d: Where raw goods like oil, gold, wheat and rubber, and futures contracts on them, are traded.
cards.x: Oil futures = commodities market.

cards.d: Market for contracts whose value comes from an underlying asset: options, futures, swaps.
cards.x: Options = derivatives market.

cards.d: Market for contracts that protect against losses from catastrophes and crime.
Where currencies are traded.
Financial firms from different sectors merging or offering each other's products, such as a bank merging with an insurance company.
cards.x: Different sectors = convergence. Same sector = consolidation.

cards.d: Firms in the same category merging, such as one retail bank buying another.
cards.x: Benefits include more liquid capital and economies of scale.

cards.d: A convergence strategy where a bank sells insurance products.
cards.x: Exam clue: a bank selling insurance to its own customers is bancassurance.

cards.d: One firm offering banking, insurance and investments: a financial supermarket.
cards.x: Made possible by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999.

cards.d: Expansion, peak, contraction (recession), trough.
cards.x: Heavy investment in new plants and equipment signals producers expect consumer spending to rise.

cards.d: GDP, hiring and spending decline.
cards.x: Stock prices tend to fall in contractions.

cards.d: High unemployment means lower output and spending, so stock prices usually decrease.
Defensive industries (utilities, groceries, healthcare) stay fairly steady through all phases. Cyclical ones (cars, travel) swing with the economy.
cards.x: Business cycles affect industries differently.

cards.d: Higher rates mean bond prices fall and borrowing costs more, which can slow stocks.
cards.x: Bond prices move opposite to interest rates.

cards.d: A rise in the general price level that erodes purchasing power. Measured by the CPI.
Bull: prices rising. Bear: prices down 20% or more from a recent high.
Money and investment flowing freely across borders.
cards.x: Brings diversification and growth, plus contagion and currency risk.

cards.d: Fast-growing developing economies. High potential growth but more instability and volatility.
cards.x: Foreign investment can fund a developing country's economic and social development.

cards.d: Investors' preference for domestic stocks while ignoring the benefits of foreign diversification.
cards.x: Driven by the higher perceived risk of investing abroad.

cards.d: Markets prefer stability. A surprise election or unrest usually decreases a country's currency value, at least for a while.
Price of one currency in another. A strong dollar makes imports cheaper and US exports pricier abroad.
Yearly report to shareholders with audited financial statements, management's discussion and the auditor's opinion.
cards.x: One of the most valuable sources of company financial data.

cards.d: SEC filings: the 10-K is the detailed annual report, the 10-Q is quarterly.
cards.x: Found free on the SEC's EDGAR database.

cards.d: SEC filing that reports major unscheduled events, such as a merger, a CEO leaving or bankruptcy, within a few business days.
cards.x: Unexpected event = 8-K.

cards.d: Document describing a new security offering and its risks.
cards.x: Companies selling securities must disclose the risks.

cards.d: Assets minus liabilities, read from the balance sheet.
Highest and lowest prices over the past year.
cards.x: A wide range indicates volatility.

cards.d: Annual dividend per share, and dividend as a percentage of price.
cards.x: A blank dividend column means the company doesn't currently pay dividends.

cards.t: Stock table: Open, Close, Net change
cards.d: Open: first trade price of the day. Close: last trade price. Net change: close compared with yesterday's close.
P/E: price divided by earnings per share. Volume: number of shares traded that day.
Average price over a set number of days, smoothing out daily noise. A rising line means an uptrend.
Compares a stock to the overall market. Rising means the stock is outperforming the market.
cards.x: A stock can be rising but falling behind the market.

cards.d: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future, because today's dollar can earn interest.
FV = PV x (1 + i)^n, where i is the interest rate and n is the number of periods.
cards.x: The interest rate and number of years are the two drivers of growth.

cards.d: PV = FV / (1 + i)^n. How much to invest today to reach a goal.
cards.x: Compounding finds future value. Discounting finds present value.

cards.d: Simple: interest on the original principal only (P x r x t). Compound: interest on principal plus earned interest.
cards.x: $1,200 at 10% for 1 year: interest $120, FV $1,320.

cards.d: 72 divided by the interest rate is roughly the number of years for money to double.
cards.x: At 8%, about 9 years.

cards.d: A series of equal payments at regular intervals, such as loan payments.
Medium of exchange, unit of measure (account) and store of value.
cards.x: Saving money for later = store of value.

cards.d: Cash, checks, debit, credit, electronic funds transfer, contactless payments and digital wallets.
cards.x: Contactless purchasing uses cards stored in a digital wallet.

cards.d: Digital currency that isn't issued or controlled by any government or bank (decentralized). Transactions are recorded on a blockchain.
Earned: wages, salary, tips. Passive or investment income: interest, dividends, rent, capital gains.
cards.x: Both are taxed. Earned income also has payroll (FICA) taxes taken out.

cards.d: An arrangement to buy now and pay later.
cards.x: Builds credit history and enables big purchases, but costs interest.

cards.d: Character, capacity, capital, collateral, conditions: how lenders judge a borrower.
Secured loans are backed by collateral. Unsecured loans aren't and charge higher rates.
Annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of borrowing, including fees. Required by the Truth in Lending Act.
Payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of history (15%), new credit (10%), credit mix (10%).
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.
cards.x: Example: "Save $6,000 for an emergency fund by December 2027 by setting aside $250 a month."

cards.d: Fixed are the same each month (rent). Variable change month to month (groceries, gas).
Assets minus liabilities.
Term covers a set period, is cheap and has no cash value. Ordinary (whole) life pays on death whenever it happens and builds cash value.
Premium (what you pay), deductible (paid before coverage starts), beneficiary (who receives the payout), claim (request for payment).
Preparing financial data for internal users (managers) to plan, control and decide. Not bound by GAAP.
cards.x: Financial accounting records history for outsiders. Managerial accounting interprets data for decisions.

cards.d: Accumulate data on costs and profits, build budgets, run cost and profitability analyses.
Can be traced to one product or project, like materials and production labor.
Shared costs that can't easily be traced to one product, like electricity, rent and IT.
cards.x: Electricity is the classic indirect cost.

cards.d: Fixed costs stay the same as volume changes (rent, salaries). Variable costs change with volume (materials, commissions).
Money already spent that can't be recovered.
cards.x: Ignore sunk costs when deciding.

cards.d: The difference in cost between two options.
cards.x: Option A costs $4,000 and B costs $5,500: differential cost $1,500.

cards.d: Value of the best alternative you give up.
Comparing the added benefit vs the added cost of one more unit or one change in activity.
cards.x: Keep going while marginal benefit is greater than marginal cost.

cards.d: Comparing planned (budgeted or forecast) results to actual results and finding why they differ.
cards.x: Use it to spot trends and fix future estimates, like re-estimating labor and time for projects.

cards.d: Favorable: revenue above budget or costs below. Unfavorable: the reverse.
Managerial accounting that captures the total cost of production: variable, fixed and operating costs.
cards.x: Purpose: find the root causes of variances and improve efficiency.

cards.d: Direct materials, direct labor and manufacturing overhead budgets.
Assigning costs to cost objects like products, departments or regions.
The activity that causes a cost, such as machine hours or square footage, used to allocate overhead.
A financial plan for a future period that sets targets for income and spending.
cards.x: The budget is the yardstick for measuring actual results.

cards.d: A static (fixed) budget doesn't adjust for activity levels. A flexible budget adjusts to actual volume.
cards.x: Weakness of a static budget: no adjustment when activity changes.

cards.d: Bottom-up: department managers build their own budgets, which roll up. Top-down: leadership sets totals.
cards.x: Bottom-up gives managers ownership of their budget, a good fix for overspending.

cards.d: Cost center, revenue center, profit center, investment center.
cards.x: Judge managers only on costs they control.

cards.d: Contribution margin = price minus variable cost per unit. Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin.
cards.x: Not on your FTDM list, but useful in roleplays.

cards.d: Collecting, storing, analyzing and reporting financial data to guide strategic decisions like budget allocation.
cards.x: Main purpose: accurate reports so managers make sound decisions.

cards.d: Comparing your financial performance with competitors or industry standards.
cards.x: Identifies weaknesses and opportunities for improvement.

cards.d: After a merger, the two companies' systems and data structures often don't match.
cards.x: Exam clue: mergers often disrupt financial-information systems until the two companies' data is combined.

cards.d: Data that is accurate, complete and consistent over its life.
Record of every step of each transaction from start to finish.
cards.x: Helps identify inconsistencies and fraud.

cards.d: Making sure a company's financial resources are used appropriately and ethically to serve its mission.
A situation where you can't be truly impartial.
cards.x: The right move: disclose the connection and remove yourself from the assignment.

cards.d: Honest, transparent reporting builds investor trust and makes raising money easier.
Laws require businesses to keep certain financial records for set periods, so they need storage strategies.
cards.x: The IRS generally says to keep tax records for 3 years, and up to 7 years in some cases.

cards.d: Protecting client and company financial data from unauthorized access.
Software that captures data automatically, reducing manual entry errors like typos and transposed numbers.
Accessible anywhere and scalable, but they increase exposure to unauthorized access and cyberattacks.
cards.x: Main downside: cybersecurity breach risk.

cards.d: Software or hardware that blocks unauthorized users from a network.
Security software kept up to date, encryption, multi-factor authentication, access controls and off-site backups.
Enterprise resource planning: one integrated system for accounting, inventory, HR and sales.
QuickBooks, Xero and similar tools automate journal entries, invoicing, payroll and reports.
Tagging financial data so computers can read it. Used in SEC filings.
Used to spot anomalies, detect fraud and forecast.
Comparing the same line item across periods: "sales rose 8% from last year."
Each line as a percentage of a base: revenue on the income statement, total assets on the balance sheet.
cards.x: Lets you compare companies of different sizes.

cards.d: Using relationships between numbers to judge liquidity, profitability, leverage and efficiency.
Current assets / current liabilities. Can the company pay its short-term bills?
(Current assets minus inventory) / current liabilities.
cards.x: Can it cover immediate liabilities without selling inventory?

cards.d: Total liabilities / shareholders' equity. How much is financed by debt instead of owners' money.
cards.x: Used to assess the risk of investing in a company.

cards.d: Money left after all costs are subtracted from revenue. Net margin = net income / revenue.

cards.t: Return on assets and return on equity
cards.d: ROA = net income / total assets. ROE = net income / equity.
Credit reports and scores, the five Cs, debt-to-income, payment history and a business customer's ratios.
cards.x: Businesses set credit standards to decide who gets credit.

cards.d: Criteria a business uses to decide which customers to extend credit to.
Software to build budgets, compare them to actuals and run what-if scenarios.
cards.x: Benefit: model unlimited scenarios to see the impact of decisions.

cards.d: Projects the cash coming in and going out during a period, to spot shortfalls early.
Spreadsheets, databases and software that make analysis faster: ratios, forecasts, dashboards.
Comparing employee addresses and phone numbers with vendor records in payables can reveal fake vendors or conflicts of interest.
SUM, AVERAGE, IF, VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP, PMT, FV, PV, NPV, IRR, pivot tables.
Maximizing customer value while minimizing waste.
Data-driven method to reduce variation and defects and improve quality. Steps: DMAIC (define, measure, analyze, improve, control).
cards.x: Lessens inefficiencies and identifies problem areas.

cards.d: Assigns overhead to products by the activities that actually use it, not by volume.
cards.x: Gives a more accurate picture of each product's profitability.

cards.d: Reporting a company's environmental, social and economic impact (ESG, or the triple bottom line of people, planet, profit).
cards.x: Can include the costs of managing climate-related risks, putting dollar figures on environmental and social risks.

cards.d: The chance of loss or of a different outcome than expected.
Pure: only loss is possible (fire). Insurable. Speculative: loss or gain is possible (investing). Not insurable.
An event or situation that can injure people or damage property or the environment.
Avoid it, reduce (control) it, transfer it (insurance, contracts) or retain (accept) it.
Identify risks, assess likelihood and impact, choose a response, implement it, monitor and review.
cards.x: First step of a risk plan: identify as many known risks as possible.

cards.d: Honestly disclosing risks and not shifting them to customers by deception.
cards.x: Hiding safety flaws in fine print is unethical risk management.

cards.d: The risk that a company can't live up to its own code of ethics, plus losses and reputation damage from cutting corners like using poor-quality materials.
Processes huge amounts of data to quantify risk and run predictive models.
cards.x: Machine learning can flag unusual transactions that humans might miss.

cards.d: Simulating possible outcomes using historical data, probabilities and expert predictions.
Regular backups stored off-site limit losses from outages, fire or cyberattacks.
Staying compliant with laws, using contracts to assign responsibility, following OSHA safety rules and insurance regulations.
Requires public companies to establish, maintain and report on internal controls over financial reporting. CEOs and CFOs certify the statements.
An insurance company set up and owned by a parent company to insure the parent's own risks.
Actions that reduce how often or how badly losses happen.
cards.x: Example: implementing and monitoring safety policies.

cards.d: Policies and procedures that prevent and detect errors and fraud.
cards.x: Example: two employees must sign any transaction over $10,000.

cards.d: Dividing tasks so no one person controls a whole transaction, such as approving, paying and recording.
Risks from outside the company that it can't control, such as inflation, tax increases, recessions and natural disasters.
cards.x: Tax increases are uncontrollable and uninsurable.

cards.d: Managing all risks across the whole organization in one integrated framework, not department by department.
cards.x: Weakness: relies heavily on management's estimates and inputs.

cards.d: A list of all of an organization's critical, enterprise-wide risks.
Strategic: risk from big decisions and long-term goals, like product positioning and competition. Operational: risk from daily processes, people and systems failing.
Someone legally required to act in another person's best interest, like a financial advisor or a board of directors.
Trading a company's stock using material, non-public information. Illegal.
A broker or analyst trades ahead of a big client's pending order to profit from the price move.
Hyping a cheap stock (often online) to push its price up, then selling before it crashes.
Paying earlier investors with new investors' money instead of real profits.
Members make money mainly by recruiting new members, and money funnels up to a few at the top.
A scammer targets members of a group they belong to or claim to belong to, like a church or community.
Securities Act of 1933 (register and disclose new securities). Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (created the SEC, regulates trading).
Gramm-Leach-Bliley (financial privacy and consolidation), Sarbanes-Oxley (internal controls), Dodd-Frank (after 2008, created the CFPB), Bank Secrecy Act and USA PATRIOT Act (anti-money laundering).
Profit or loss from selling an investment. Losses can offset gains for tax purposes.
cards.x: Short-term gains (1 year or less) are taxed as ordinary income. Long-term gains get lower rates.

cards.d: Tax on nonessential, expensive goods like high-end cars and jewelry.
Tax on the value of assets transferred at death.
cards.x: Property passing directly to a surviving spouse is generally exempt.

cards.d: Donations to qualified charities can be tax-deductible.
Interest paid on debt is tax-deductible; dividends aren't. That encourages companies to use debt.
Following laws plus internal and external regulations.
cards.x: Builds public trust and keeps financial institutions stable.

cards.d: Its job is preventing violations, then detecting and correcting them.
cards.x: Prevention comes first.

cards.d: Fines, audits, lawsuits and a damaged reputation.
Automates monitoring, reporting and record-keeping.
cards.x: Reduces compliance costs and identifies patterns and trends.

cards.d: Offer, acceptance, consideration (something of value exchanged), capacity, legality.
An agent acts for the principal and must act in the principal's best interest.
Sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, S corp, LLC, nonprofit (primary goal is a mission, not profit).
The system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled for its shareholders and stakeholders.
cards.x: In short: who makes decisions, how those decisions are checked, and who the decision makers answer to.

cards.d: Minimizes unethical behavior, reduces risk, prevents mismanagement and builds investor confidence.
cards.x: Poor governance lowers investor confidence and limits profitability.

cards.d: Elected by shareholders to govern the corporation. A fiduciary for the shareholders.
cards.x: Sets overall strategic direction, protects shareholders' investments, hires and oversees the CEO, approves governance policies.

cards.d: Board members with no ties to management, who can oversee objectively.
Board committee of independent directors that oversees financial reporting and the auditors.
Formal written standards of ethical behavior for all employees.
cards.x: A direct way to build a culture of integrity.

cards.d: A corporation's internal rulebook: how it's run, how decisions are made, shareholder rights.
A company's own review of its controls and governance practices.
cards.x: Ensures governance practices are sound and issues get addressed.

cards.d: Independent CPA firm's review of whether the financial statements are accurate and fairly presented.
cards.x: Focus: proving the accuracy of the financial statements.

cards.d: Processes that make reporting reliable, prevent fraud and keep the company compliant.
cards.x: Separation of duties is the classic example.

cards.d: Sharing accurate, timely information with shareholders and the public.
Managers (agents) may act in their own interest instead of the owners' (principals).
cards.x: Governance aligns them through board oversight and pay tied to performance.

cards.d: Controls inside the company: board, bylaws, internal audit, code of conduct, pay policies.
Controls from outside: government regulations (SEC, SOX), external auditors, stock exchange rules, activist investors.
Going public (strict regulation, high transparency), growth, new laws, ownership changes, scandals such as a director charged with fraud.
Anyone affected by the company: shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, community, lenders.
The board guides decision-making so the company pursues its mission efficiently and ethically. Adds approvals and checks.
Follow the code of conduct, report wrongdoing, keep accurate records, avoid conflicts of interest.
cards.x: When employees see how their role serves company goals, they feel a greater sense of purpose.

cards.d: An employee who reports wrongdoing. Protected from retaliation under SOX and Dodd-Frank.
Banking, accounting, corporate finance, insurance, securities and investments, personal financial planning.
cards.x: Accounting careers involve financial documents, spreadsheets and bookkeeping.

cards.d: Develops investment strategies and oversees portfolios for clients.
Brokers, traders, analysts and investment bankers. High pay, but very stressful with long hours.
Financial planners and advisors helping individuals manage money, save and invest toward goals.
Loan officer, credit analyst, underwriter (judges risk for loans or insurance), actuary (insurance math), claims adjuster, auditor, compliance officer, controller, treasurer, CFO.
CPA (accounting), CFA (investment analysis), CFP (financial planning). FINRA licenses: Series 7 and Series 63.
Building professional relationships that bring information, referrals and opportunities.
cards.x: The main payoff of a network: information, referrals and opportunities you wouldn't find alone.

cards.d: AICPA, CFA Institute, Financial Planning Association, American Bankers Association.
cards.x: Joining lets you serve on committees, hold offices and attend seminars.

cards.d: National conferences build broad contact networks. Hosting finance seminars for small businesses brings new clients.
A structured way to get happy clients to recommend you.
cards.x: A happy client referring friends is the payoff of great service.

cards.d: Informal time, like a round of golf with a vendor, helps you get to know contacts.
Give appropriate, suitable advice, keep information confidential, avoid or disclose conflicts of interest, provide services clients can't get on their own, understand client expectations.
Recommending only products that fit the client's goals, risk tolerance and situation.
Verifying a client's identity, finances and goals before serving them.
Strategies, processes, people and technology to build long-term customer value.
cards.x: Purpose: provide products and services customers want.

cards.d: Software that puts all customer data and interactions in a single hub, like Salesforce or HubSpot.
cards.x: Reveals sales opportunities and customers' prior purchases.

cards.d: CRM collects huge amounts of data, so people must tell useful information from unnecessary information.
Sorting large data sets to find patterns, then analyzing and visualizing the results.
cards.x: Two prediction types: regression (predicts a number) and classification (predicts a category).

cards.d: Organized collection of data. Field = one data item, record = one complete entry, table = a set of records.
A request for specific data from a database, using criteria.
cards.x: To find Springdale customers with purchases over $100,000, set criteria on both the address and amount fields.

cards.d: Pinpoint exactly what question you want the database to answer.
Selecting a smaller subset of data for analysis using criteria.
cards.x: Filter broad to narrow: industry, then country, then analyst rating.

cards.d: Restructuring a database to reduce redundancy (duplicate data) and improve data integrity.
Primary key: unique ID for each record. Foreign key: links one table to another.
Data stored in related tables linked by keys. Queried with SQL.
In many naturally occurring data sets, the leading digit is small: 1 leads about 30% of the time, 9 under 5%.
cards.x: Used to detect fraud. Works only on data that is measured, not assigned (not phone numbers or IDs). Fabricated data often shows digits appearing about equally.

cards.d: System that collects and reports data to support decision-making.
Official documented evidence of a company's transactions and financial activities.
CRM and sales records show customers' prior purchases and preferences.
Collecting information about outside factors.
cards.x: Political: laws and regulations. Economic: interest rates, taxes. Social: family roles. Technological.

cards.d: Finding patterns and relationships in large data sets.
cards.x: Rule induction finds if-then relationships.

cards.d: Using people's data without their knowledge, like their search history for targeted ads, raises privacy concerns.
Primary: collected for your purpose. Secondary: already exists.
Average; middle value; most frequent value.
Recognizing and managing your own emotions and others'. Self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
